v.why: Under standard parameterization, wide layers sum many Adam-sized updates over fan-in, so raising the LR pushes wide nets into divergence sooner.
Widening at high LR enlarges the function-space update per step, turning a usually helpful capacity gain into instability.
The L2 term is scaled by alpha over the minibatch size and applied every step, so with batches of 4-10 extra alpha becomes a very strong decay that causes underfitting.
Because the L2 term is divided by batch size and applied once per step, a larger batch relieves over-regularization when alpha is strong.
Tiny batches already give many noisy updates, so a higher LR adds little optimization progress but crosses the noise-driven stability threshold sooner.
At tiny LRs progress is limited by step count, so the fewer updates from a larger batch compound into severe under-training.
Deeper nets need more optimization progress, so with a tiny LR an extra layer leaves the network under-trained within 243 epochs.
Shallow nets have better-conditioned loss landscapes that tolerate larger steps, so raising the LR is less harmful or more helpful than in deeper nets.
L2 shrinkage applied to every layer compounds multiplicatively through three layers and attenuates the forward signal more than in shallow nets.
A single hidden layer can add capacity only through width, whereas deeper nets already gain capacity through composition, so width matters more when shallow.
